subject: WSJ Politics: Trump Sees New World Order, But Strains Only Worsen

96 Plus, the president’s family to be targeted by congressional probes, and lawmakers grill administration officials over threats to the homeland   Is this email difficult to read? View in browser             Sponsored by       Damian Paletta   Trump Sees New World Order, But Strains Only Worsen   Plus, the president’s family to be targeted by congressional probes, and lawmakers grill administration officials over threats to the homeland     IORI SAGISAWA/CHINA POOL/GETTY IMAGES   Good morning. When President Trump took office for the second time last year, he launched an ambitious effort to bend dusty and tired international institutions to his will and create a New World Order.

   Out: G-20, G-7, NATO, United Nations, USMCA.

   In: Russia, China, North Korea, Argentina, El Salvador, Hungary, Israel, Saudi Arabia and a post-Maduro Venezuela.

   It worked, for a while. But now, as he has perhaps his weakest domestic standing of either presidency, Trump’s international power and leverage might be contracting as well. Is he reaching deals, forging treaties or conducting photo ops? And some of those new alliances are either proving ephemeral or struggling amid their own domestic pressures.

   Trump met with Russia’s Vladimir Putin and China’s Xi Jinping on Thursday. He has also floated the possibility of meeting with North Korea’s Kim Jong Un while on this trip.

   To what end? The GOP was pulverized in the midterm elections, and Trump will have much less leeway to appease Russia in its war with Ukraine next year. Similarly, the Nvidia scandal has raised a heap of questions about the White House’s AI policy AND its China policy.

   Trump, meanwhile, is going out of his way to befriend Xi, as opposed to his first term when he was constantly looking for leverage. Will this lead to new jobs in the U.S.? New Chinese investment in the U.S.? The export of more semiconductor chips to China?

   This could all come to a head in December, when Trump hosts the Group of 20 summit in southern Florida. The Old World Order (Europe, Canada, Mexico, Japan) should be there, as will members of this New World Order. Trump will be the host, weakened politically but creating a spectacle for the ages.

   One question they must all be wondering is: What happens to this world order in the post-Trump era? Will the next U.S. president, Democrat or Republican, have the same fondness for these countries that Trump has?

   This is an edition of the Politics newsletter, bringing you an expert guide to what’s driving D.C. every day. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here . 

       People and Policies I’m Watching   Hakeem Jeffries: The New York congressman looks set to be the next House speaker after he was nominated for the job by fellow Democrats.

   Trump’s Thursday: The president will make his way back to Washington, D.C., after wrapping up his Asia trip.

       CONTENT FROM: ELEVANCE HEALTH     Sustainable Innovation in Healthcare   How emerging technology and streamlining the patient care experience are solving complex healthcare challenges.   Watch Now  >       What I’m Following     DOUG MILLS/POOL/GETTY IMAGES   Trump said history was being made at the first-ever summit with the leaders of China and Russia. At the 90-minute meeting, there was little indication of progress on the major issues brought to the table: the wars in Ukraine and Iran and the proliferation of nuclear weapons. But for the men in the spotlight, just sitting down together was the point.

   Trump’s family is targeted by the incoming House Oversight Committee chair. Democrat Robert Garcia is planning investigations into the president’s family , as well as current and former Trump administration officials. Garcia has sent 12 letters representing formal notices to preserve records and answer questions for pending congressional investigations on four subjects covering what he described as: Trump family corruption, corporate corruption, DHS misconduct and the Epstein coverup.

   Lawmakers question Markwayne Mullin and Jay Clayton about threats to the U.S. homeland. Members of the House Homeland Security committee asked Mullin, the Homeland Security Secretary, and the Director of National Intelligence about recent network outages and the threat posed by Iran. Here are the Journal’s takeaways from the session.

       What Else Is Happening   • Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth made an unexpected visit to Caracas, signing a military pact with Venezuela’s interim government.

   • The Jensen Huang saga has reinvigorated Washington’s China hawks.

   • A top European defense chief called a Pentagon official’s criticism of Kyiv’s strikes “stupid” at a meeting aimed at boosting unity in support of Ukraine .

       What I’m Reading   • ‘It’s Not Fine’: Massive Tech Failures Fuel Alarm About U.S. Infrastructure ( Los Angeles Times )

   • Nike to Give U.S. Grads Free Shoes After Colom’s Request ( Clarion Ledger )

   • Can Van Hollen Chuck Schumer? ( New York magazine )

       Corrections & Amplifications 

   Markwayne Mullin flew to Louisiana for a prime-time college-football game. The Nov. 18 edition of this newsletter incorrectly said he flew to Texas.

       About Me   I’m Damian Paletta, The Wall Street Journal’s Washington coverage chief. I’ve covered Washington for 22 years as a reporter and editor. I’ve covered the White House, Congress, national security, the federal budget, economics and multiple market meltdowns.
